howToUse: 1. Attach or paste your programming lecture slides, lab sheet, or algorithms topic along with this JSON.
2. Instruct the AI: 'Follow _aiPrompt strictly to generate daily compiler coding challenges directly based on my slides/topic.'
3. Upload or paste the returned JSON in Compiler Questions -> Import/Export -> Import from JSON.
_aiPrompt.prompt:
You are a Senior Competitive Programming & Coding Lab Author and strict JSON generator for Quiz Platform. Based strictly on the attached programming slides, notes, or syllabus, create self-contained coding problems in strict JSON format.

PROBLEM CRAFTING QUALITY:
- Tie every problem directly to concepts taught in the attached slides (e.g., loops, arrays/lists, dictionaries/hash maps, recursion, two pointers, binary search, OOP).
- Provide clear Problem Statement, Input / Output specification, 2 concrete Worked Examples (including an edge case), and explicit Constraints.
- Write clean, idiomatic, bug-free 'referenceCode' that handles edge cases cleanly and prints or demonstrates a working call.
- Write 2-3 progressive 'hints' that nudge the student's thinking step-by-step WITHOUT giving away the full answer.

CRITICAL UI & TEXT RENDERING RULES:
- The Daily Challenge UI displays 'description' and 'hints' inside a plain pre-wrapped text block (whitespace-pre-wrap). It does NOT parse Markdown and does NOT run KaTeX!
- THEREFORE, NEVER use ### headings, **bold**, *italics*, ```code fences```, `inline backticks`, or $LaTeX$ math ($...$) anywhere inside 'title', 'description', or 'hints'!
- Format 'description' using clean plain-text headings ('Problem:', 'Example 1:', 'Example 2:', 'Constraints:'), indented lines, and Unicode math symbols (≤, ≥, ×, ≠, ->, O(N), O(log N)).

STRICT JSON OUTPUT:
- Return ONLY valid raw JSON matching { "questions": [ ... ] }. Omit '_aiPrompt'. Use only valid enum values from strictJsonContract.

CompilerQuestion.title: string (required concise problem title, max 200 chars)
CompilerQuestion.description: string (required clean PLAIN TEXT with \n formatting; NO markdown ###/**/` and NO $LaTeX$)

questions.title: Two Sum Target Finder
questions.description:
Problem:
Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the two distinct indices whose values add up to target. Every test input has exactly one valid solution, and you cannot use the same element twice.

Example 1:
  Input: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
  Output: [0, 1]   (because nums[0] + nums[1] == 9)

Example 2:
  Input: nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6
  Output: [1, 2]

Constraints:
  - 2 ≤ len(nums) ≤ 10,000
  - Target Time Complexity: O(N)
hints: Brute force nested loops take O(N^2). Can you remember previously visited values in O(1) lookup time?
Store each value's index in a Python dict as you iterate once from left to right.
Before inserting the current number, check whether (target - current) is already in your dictionary.

questions.title: Deep Flatten Array with Depth Limit
questions.description:
Problem:
Write a JavaScript function flatten(arr, depth = 1) that returns a new array flattening nested sub-arrays up to depth levels deep. Elements nested deeper than depth must remain intact as sub-arrays.

Example 1:
  Input: arr = [1, [2, [3, [4]], 5]], depth = 2
  Output: [1, 2, 3, [4], 5]

Example 2:
  Input: arr = [1, [2, 3]], depth = 0
  Output: [1, [2, 3]]

Constraints:
  - Do not mutate the original input array.
  - Handle empty nested arrays [] cleanly.
  - If depth ≤ 0, return a shallow copy of arr.
hints: Base case: when depth ≤ 0, return arr.slice() so no further unwrapping occurs.
Check Array.isArray(item) to distinguish nested sub-arrays from scalar values.
Recurse with (depth - 1) and spread or push the returned elements into the accumulator array.

questions.title: Group Anagrams by Canonical Key
questions.description:
Problem:
Write a TypeScript function groupAnagrams(words: string[]): string[][] that groups strings that are anagrams of one another into separate sub-arrays.

Example 1:
  Input: ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]
  Output: [["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]]

Example 2:
  Input: [""]
  Output: [[""]]

Constraints:
  - 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 10,000
  - Lowercase ASCII strings; group ordering may be arbitrary.
hints: Two words are anagrams if and only if they contain identical character counts.
Sorting the characters of each word creates a canonical string key shared by all its anagrams.
Use a Map<string, string[]> keyed by the sorted signature (or a 26-letter frequency key for O(K) per word).

questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.description:
Problem:
You are given an integer array nums containing distinct values originally sorted ascending, then rotated at an unknown pivot index. Return the index of target if present in nums, otherwise return -1.

Example 1:
  Input: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0
  Output: 4

Example 2:
  Input: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 3
  Output: -1

Constraints:
  - 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 5,000
  - Required Runtime Complexity: O(log N)
hints: A linear scan violates the O(log N) constraint; modify standard binary search instead.
Whenever you split at mid, at least one half ([left..mid] or [mid..right]) MUST still be strictly sorted.
Identify the sorted half by comparing nums[left] <= nums[mid], then test if target falls inside that sorted interval.
